claims.title: Unreliable stream parsing control using available() method (lines 148, 244)
claims.impact: The available() method contract does not guarantee detection of stream end for all stream types. If TruncatedInputStream or the underlying stream has unexpected behavior, the parsing loop could exit prematurely while data remains unread. This causes incomplete deserialization of AMQP tables and arrays, leaving subsequent protocol data out of sync and causing parsing errors or data corruption.
claims.evidence: Lines 148 and 244 use while(tableIn.available() > 0) and while(arrayIn.available() > 0) to control protocol message parsing loops. The available() method is documented as returning an estimate of bytes available without blocking, not as a reliable EOF indicator for bounded streams.

claims.title: SNAPSHOT Version in Release Manifest Violates Reproducibility
claims.impact: Downstream consumers receive non-reproducible builds; artifact is development-grade, not a stable release. Each build may pull different code from the repository at build time.
claims.evidence: <version>5.34.0-SNAPSHOT</version>

claims.title: Groovy 2.4.21 end-of-life dependency in build
claims.impact: Groovy 2.4 reached end of life in 2017 and receives no security patches. The groovy-maven-plugin uses this at build time to generate AMQP source files from specifications (line 596-637). Any vulnerability in Groovy 2.4 would affect all downstream builds.
claims.evidence: pom.xml line 81 declares `<groovy.all.version>2.4.21</groovy.all.version>`. Release date: March 2016. Final 2.4.x release, no further updates.

claims.title: Unbounded memory allocation in readBytes() enables denial of service
claims.impact: An attacker who controls the AMQP broker or intercepts protocol data can cause the client to attempt allocation of gigabytes of contiguous memory, triggering OutOfMemoryError and denial of service. Applies to long strings (type 'S'), byte arrays (type 'x'), and table/array payloads.
claims.evidence: Method readBytes() reads a 32-bit unsigned integer as length (line 86), then allocates a byte array without size validation: `byte [] buffer = new byte[(int)contentLength];` (line 88). The condition `contentLength < Integer.MAX_VALUE` (line 87) allows allocation up to 2,147,483,646 bytes.

claims.title: Jetty 9.4.58 End-of-Life Test Dependency
claims.impact: Jetty 9.4.x reached end-of-life. Latest version 11.0.x contains security hardening and bug fixes. Low immediate impact because Jetty is used only in test scope, not production.
claims.evidence: <jetty.version>9.4.58.v20250814</jetty.version>

claims.title: Unbounded byte array allocation enables denial of service
claims.impact: An attacker can craft an AMQP frame with a contentLength value equal or close to Integer.MAX_VALUE (2,147,483,647). This causes immediate OutOfMemoryError when the JVM attempts to allocate the array, resulting in denial of service. The application crashes without processing the message.
claims.evidence: readBytes() method at line 83 reads an unsigned 32-bit integer at line 86: final long contentLength = unsignedExtend(in.readInt()). This value is then used directly to allocate a byte array at line 88: final byte[] buffer = new byte[(int)contentLength]. No bounds checking is performed on contentLength before allocation.

claims.title: Potential integer overflow in timestamp conversion
claims.impact: A malformed AMQP frame with a timestamp value close to Long.MAX_VALUE will cause silent integer overflow, resulting in a Date object with an incorrect (negative) timestamp. This could cause unexpected behavior in code relying on timestamp ordering or comparisons.
claims.evidence: Line 269: `return new Date(in.readLong()*1000);` multiplies an untrusted network-supplied long value by 1000 without overflow checking. If the input long value is close to Long.MAX_VALUE/1000 (approximately 9.22e15), the multiplication will overflow and produce a negative date.

claims.title: Integer overflow in timestamp multiplication without bounds checking
claims.impact: An attacker sending a malicious AMQP protocol message with a specially crafted timestamp value could cause integer overflow, resulting in a Date object with an incorrect time value. This could potentially be exploited in business logic that relies on timestamp ordering or validity, or could cause unexpected behavior in code that assumes timestamp validity.
claims.evidence: At line 269, the code reads an 8-byte long from the network and multiplies it by 1000 without overflow checking: `return new Date(in.readLong()*1000);`. If the long value read from the network is greater than Long.MAX_VALUE / 1000 (approximately 9223372036854775), the multiplication will silently overflow, wrapping to a negative value or causing unexpected behavior in Date constructor.

claims.title: Integer overflow in timestamp conversion (line 269)
claims.impact: An attacker sending a crafted AMQP message with a malicious timestamp value causes integer overflow in the multiplication operation, resulting in a Date object with an incorrect wrapped-around time value. This could disrupt application logic dependent on message timestamps, including message expiration, scheduling, and time-based authorization.
claims.evidence: Line 269: return new Date(in.readLong()*1000); reads a 64-bit long from untrusted AMQP wire protocol data, multiplies by 1000, and passes to Date constructor without overflow checking. A timestamp value greater than 9223372036854775L causes multiplication to overflow.

claims.title: Unbounded Buffer Allocation in readBytes() Permits Denial of Service
claims.impact: An attacker can craft an AMQP message with a length-prefixed field claiming up to 2.1GB of data. The client will attempt to allocate a 2.1GB byte array, causing OutOfMemoryError and denial of service.

claims.title: Integer overflow in timestamp conversion calculation
claims.impact: An attacker can provide a timestamp value that causes integer overflow during the multiplication by 1000, resulting in a Date with an incorrect or negative millisecond value. This could cause incorrect time-based operations, logging anomalies, or business logic errors in code that relies on the timestamp. While not direct code execution, it can corrupt application state.
claims.evidence: readTimestamp() method at line 266 contains: return new Date(in.readLong()*1000). The long value read from the stream is multiplied by 1000 without overflow checking. If in.readLong() returns a value greater than Long.MAX_VALUE / 1000 (approximately 9,223,372,036,854), the multiplication wraps around, creating an incorrect timestamp.

claims.title: Silent Type Corruption in readFieldValue() Error Reporting
claims.impact: Attacker sends an AMQP message with an invalid type byte (e.g., 0xFF). The exception is thrown but does not include the actual byte value, making debugging difficult. Attackers can craft messages that trigger cryptic errors, potentially used for protocol confusion or information gathering.
claims.evidence:
default:
    throw new MalformedFrameException("Unrecognised type in table");

claims.title: Unbounded recursion in readFieldValue() enables stack exhaustion denial of service
claims.impact: An attacker can craft an AMQP message with nested tables and arrays to a depth exceeding available stack frames (typically 500-1000 on Java), causing StackOverflowError and denial of service. The recursion depth is unbounded and depends only on payload construction.
claims.evidence: Method readFieldValue() (line 158) recursively calls itself indirectly: case 'F' (line 181) calls readTable() which calls readFieldValue() (line 150); case 'A' (line 184) calls readArray() which calls readFieldValue() (line 245). No recursion depth limit is enforced. A protocol message with deeply nested table→array→table→... structures will exhaust stack space.

claims.title: Inefficient BigInteger construction enables algorithmic complexity attack
claims.impact: While the current code is limited to 4-byte unscaled values for BigDecimal, the pattern of constructing BigInteger from untrusted byte arrays without length validation is problematic. In general, large BigInteger objects can consume significant CPU during arithmetic operations (CWE-407). An attacker providing large unscaled values (via extension of the protocol) could cause algorithmic complexity attacks.
claims.evidence: readFieldValue() method handles case 'D' (BigDecimal) at line 171. It reads a 1-byte scale at line 172, then reads 4 bytes into an array at line 173-174, and constructs: value = new BigInteger(unscaled), scale); at line 175. The byte array length is fixed at 4 bytes in this case, but the BigInteger constructor can be exploited if this pattern were used elsewhere with variable-length input.

claims.title: Unbounded recursive deserialization allows stack exhaustion
claims.impact: An attacker who can send AMQP protocol messages to the client can craft a message with deeply nested tables/arrays that triggers a StackOverflowError, causing the client process to crash. This is a denial-of-service attack that terminates the client connection handler.
claims.evidence: The readFieldValue() method (line 158-221) is recursive. It calls readTable() at line 181 for case 'F', and readArray() at line 184 for case 'A'. The readTable() method (lines 139-155) calls readFieldValue() again (line 150). The readArray() method (lines 237-249) also calls readFieldValue() again (line 245). There is no recursion depth limit checked in any of these methods. A malicious AMQP message containing deeply nested tables or arrays (e.g., a table containing an array containing a table containing an array...) will exhaust the Java stack and cause StackOverflowError.

claims.title: Denial of service via unbounded byte array allocation
claims.impact: A remote attacker can craft an AMQP frame with a large contentLength value to consume all available heap memory, causing the Java process to crash or become unresponsive. This is a direct denial of service attack.
claims.evidence: Lines 86-90: The method reads a 32-bit unsigned integer from the network and uses it to allocate a byte array. The code `if(contentLength < Integer.MAX_VALUE)` allows allocation of up to Integer.MAX_VALUE - 1 bytes (approximately 2 GB). An attacker sending a frame with contentLength near 2 GB will exhaust available heap memory, causing OutOfMemoryError and denial of service.

claims.title: Unbounded recursive parsing enables stack overflow denial of service
claims.impact: An attacker providing a malicious AMQP frame with deeply nested table or array structures can exhaust the stack, causing StackOverflowError and denial of service. Example: a table containing a field with type 'F' (another table), which itself contains a field with type 'F', nested to arbitrary depth.
claims.evidence: readTable() method at line 139 recursively calls readFieldValue() at line 150. readFieldValue() at line 158 switches on type byte and calls readTable() again at line 181 (case 'F') and readArray() at line 184 (case 'A'). readArray() at line 237 recursively calls readFieldValue() at line 245. No depth limit is enforced on recursion.

claims.title: Unbounded Recursion in readTable() and readArray() Permits Stack Overflow
claims.impact: An attacker can craft an AMQP message containing tables nested 10,000+ levels deep. Each level consumes stack frame space. This causes StackOverflowException and denial of service.

claims.title: Hardcoded GPG Key ID in Source Control Enables Key Enumeration
claims.impact: GPG key ID exposure enables attackers to enumerate which key was used for signing. If the key is later compromised, attackers can forge past releases or retroactively sign malicious artifacts using the known key ID.
claims.evidence: <gpg.keyname>6026DFCA</gpg.keyname>

claims.title: Unvalidated UTF-8 string decoding from untrusted wire data
claims.impact: An attacker sending malformed UTF-8 sequences in AMQP messages could cause silent data corruption or inconsistent state if the application logic depends on exact string matching. This is low-impact because Java's String class does not execute code from the input and will only produce characters, but semantic attacks are possible if the application trusts field names or routing keys.
claims.evidence: The readShortstr() method at line 70 constructs a String from raw bytes using the 'utf-8' charset without validating that the input is well-formed UTF-8. The byte array length is read as a single unsigned byte (line 68), limiting maximum short-string length to 255 bytes. If an AMQP peer sends malformed UTF-8 sequences, the String constructor may accept replacement characters.

claims.title: Stack overflow from unbounded recursive deserialization of nested tables and arrays
claims.impact: A malicious AMQP server or a man-in-the-middle attacker can crash any client using this library by sending a crafted protocol message with deeply nested nested tables/arrays, causing denial of service.
claims.evidence: The readFieldValue() method at line 158 recursively deserializes untrusted AMQP protocol data. Case 'F' at line 181 calls readTable(), which at line 150 calls readFieldValue() again. Case 'A' at line 184 calls readArray(), which at line 245 calls readFieldValue() again. An attacker can craft a protocol message with deeply nested tables and arrays (e.g., table containing array containing table containing array...) to trigger unbounded recursion and exhaust stack memory, causing StackOverflowError.

claims.title: Potential OutOfMemoryError from large buffer allocation
claims.impact: A malformed or hostile AMQP message declaring a content length near Integer.MAX_VALUE (~2GB) causes OutOfMemoryError, denying service to the client
claims.evidence: Line 86-94: check `if(contentLength < Integer.MAX_VALUE)` permits allocation of arrays up to Integer.MAX_VALUE bytes, line 88: `final byte [] buffer = new byte[(int)contentLength];`

claims.title: Deprecated String constructor with implicit charset
claims.impact: Deprecated API; potential for charset mismatch on systems where platform default is not UTF-8, though explicit charset string provides some protection. The constructor itself is deprecated as of Java 6 and throws IllegalCharsetNameException or UnsupportedCharsetException if the string argument is not a valid charset name.
claims.evidence: Line 70: `new String(b, "utf-8")` uses deprecated constructor that relies on platform default if exception occurs

claims.title: Integer overflow in timestamp multiplication
claims.impact: Multiplying a long timestamp by 1000 can overflow the range when the input value is close to Long.MAX_VALUE, resulting in Date objects with incorrect or negative timestamps
claims.evidence: Line 269: `return new Date(in.readLong()*1000);` multiplies a long by 1000 without overflow checking

claims.title: Groovy Build Dependency EOL Without Security Updates
claims.impact: Groovy 2.4.21 reached end-of-life in 2015 (9 years ago). No security patches are available. If a vulnerability is discovered in the codegen phase, it cannot be remediated.
claims.evidence: <groovy.all.version>2.4.21</groovy.all.version>

claims.title: SLF4J 1.7.36 End-of-Life Dependency
claims.impact: SLF4J 1.7.36 reached end-of-life in October 2022. Later versions (2.0+) include bug fixes and security hardening. Using EOL versions increases exposure to known issues.
claims.evidence: <slf4j.version>1.7.36</slf4j.version>
